longForm.title: Dien Bien Phu, 1954: The Valley That Ended France's War
longForm.excerpt: General Navarre chose Dien Bien Phu to force a decisive battle. General Giap dragged artillery through mountains the French said were impassable, and in 55 days dismantled the largest French fortress in Indochina.
paragraphs: The valley at Dien Bien Phu is twelve kilometers long and eight wide, ringed on all sides by jungle-covered hills. Colonel Christian de Castries surveyed it from the air in November 1953 and called it perfect. It was flat enough for an airstrip. It was remote enough to attract a large Viet Minh force. The hills were close enough that artillery on them could cover the valley floor — his artillery, in Castries's understanding, positioned inside the perimeter to suppress any guns the enemy managed to drag forward. What the French failed to adequately weigh was that those same hills gave an enemy with artillery the ability to fire downward into everything they were building. General Henri Navarre's headquarters had assessed the terrain as impassable for heavy weapons. General Vo Nguyen Giap had 50,000 men and a different assessment.

Navarre's plan had a name — Plan Navarre — and a logic that was not entirely unreasonable given what he knew. The Viet Minh had proven capable of guerrilla operations and mobile ambushes but had not yet demonstrated the sustained ability to assault prepared positions at scale. A fortified base in the northwest, drawing Giap into exactly that kind of frontal assault, would allow French firepower to break the Viet Minh against the wire. The base was divided into strong points, each given a woman's name: Beatrice, Gabrielle, Dominique, Eliane, Isabelle, Huguette. Colonel Charles Piroth commanded the French artillery. Before the assault began, he assured his commanders that any Viet Minh gun that showed itself would be destroyed within minutes. He put it in writing.

Giap opened his assault on March 13, 1954. The first target was Beatrice, the northern strongpoint held by the 3rd Battalion of the French Foreign Legion's 13th Demi-Brigade — one of the best infantry units in the French military. The Viet Minh artillery, pre-registered on French command positions, opened at 17:00 and found them immediately. Major Paul Pégot, the battalion commander, was killed in the first barrage. His replacement was killed shortly after. Beatrice fell the same night. Gabrielle, held by Algerian riflemen of the 7th Algerian Rifle Regiment, fell the following day. Colonel Piroth found that the Viet Minh guns were pre-positioned in concealed bunkers carved into the hillsides, firing through small apertures invisible from the air. French counter-battery fire could not locate them. On the night of March 14, Piroth retired to his dugout and killed himself with a grenade.

The airstrip was the decisive variable. Without it, the garrison could not be reinforced or resupplied at scale. Viet Minh anti-aircraft batteries — approximately 36 Soviet-supplied 37mm guns and hundreds of 12.7mm heavy machine guns positioned in the surrounding hills — made daylight runway operations increasingly dangerous after the first week. By late March, fixed-wing transport aircraft could no longer land in daylight. Supply drops from C-119 Flying Boxcars and C-47s became the only resupply option, and a significant portion of each drop fell outside the perimeter into Viet Minh hands. The garrison's ammunition consumption outran what drops could deliver. French requests for American air support reached the Eisenhower administration in March and April — for B-29 strikes, for carrier-based aircraft, for what was referred to internally as Operation Vulture. Eisenhower declined without British support. Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden declined to provide it.

The siege's middle phase, from late March through April, was a grinding contest of trenches. Giap adopted the method of slow approach — digging communications trenches toward the French perimeter, extending sap lines, strangling the defensive positions one by one before assaulting. French commanders recognized the method: it was standard siege practice from the seventeenth century, applied against twentieth-century fortifications. The garrison conducted sorties to interrupt the digging, losing men it could not replace. Reinforcement was attempted by parachute: some of the paratroopers who volunteered to jump in had never made a combat drop before. Their names — the men who chose to jump into a valley everyone knew was lost — are recorded at the Mémorial des guerres en Indochine at Fréjus.

The monsoon arrived early. It flooded the trenches, flooded the medical bunkers, flooded the communication trenches the Viet Minh were pushing forward. Medical personnel operated by battery lantern in water to their ankles. The International Red Cross negotiated a 24-hour ceasefire for medical evacuation in late April. Giap refused it. The wounded numbered in the thousands. Approximately 40 seriously wounded men were evacuated by light aircraft before the runway became completely unusable. The remainder stayed. Huguette 1, the last strongpoint holding the northwestern perimeter, fell on April 22 after weeks of assault. The French defensive line contracted to a strip roughly 900 meters wide and 1,600 meters long — less than a tenth of the original perimeter.

The final assault came on the night of May 6. Viet Minh forces overran Eliane 2, the dominant height on the eastern perimeter, after detonating a mining charge tunneled under the French position over several weeks. By the morning of May 7, the last radio transmission from Castries reported his command post under direct assault. He was ordered not to surrender formally — to avoid the legal and diplomatic implications — but to cease fire. The order went out at 17:30. The battle had lasted 55 days. The Viet Minh flag went up over the French command bunker at approximately 17:50. Giap's forces had suffered an estimated 23,000 casualties — around 8,000 killed, the remainder wounded. The French garrison reported approximately 1,500 killed and 4,000 wounded. Nearly 11,000 were taken prisoner. Fewer than 3,900 returned alive from the camps.

The Geneva Conference had been running since April 26, three weeks before the fall. The French delegation's negotiating position changed on May 7. The Geneva Accords of July 1954 partitioned Vietnam at the 17th parallel, with French withdrawal from the north and a promised nationwide election in 1956 that never took place. The United States, which had been financing approximately 80 percent of France's war costs by 1954, did not sign the Accords but acknowledged them. American advisors were arriving in South Vietnam before the French completed their withdrawal. The logic that had failed at Dien Bien Phu — that the right kind of fortified position could force a decisive conventional battle and end an insurgency — would be tested again, by a different army, in the same country, for another twenty years.

shortForm.title: Gloster Hill, April 1951: 750 Men Against Three Chinese Divisions
shortForm.excerpt: On the night of April 22, 1951, the Gloucestershire Regiment held Hill 235 against elements of 30,000 Chinese soldiers for three days. Of the 750 men who started the battle, 39 made it back to UN lines.
paragraphs: On the night of April 22, 1951, approximately 30,000 soldiers of the Chinese People's Volunteer Army 63rd Army crossed the Imjin River in central Korea on a front of 30 kilometers. Their objective was Seoul, 50 kilometers to the south. Standing in part of their path, on a ridge the men called Gloster Hill and the maps called Hill 235, was the 1st Battalion, Gloucestershire Regiment — 750 men holding a position the Chinese order of battle had assigned to an entire division. The Glosters had been in Korea since September 1950 as part of the British 29th Infantry Brigade. They held for three nights.

The Chinese attacked in waves, using bugles to coordinate assaults across multiple points of the perimeter simultaneously. The Glosters called in artillery and air support and held through April 23 and into April 24, inflicting losses that the 63rd Army's after-action reports would later describe as disproportionate. By April 24, the battalion was surrounded, ammunition was critically low, and resupply helicopters could not reach the position without drawing fire. Lieutenant Colonel James Carne, commanding, kept the perimeter tight and the men fighting. A relief force from the 5th Royal Inniskilling Dragoon Guards attempted to push up the road toward Gloster Hill and was turned back by roadblocks and anti-tank fire before getting close.

On the morning of April 25, 1951, Carne ordered what remained of the battalion to break out in small groups. Of 750 men, 39 made it back to UN lines. Approximately 180 were killed in the fighting; the remaining 500-plus were taken prisoner. Carne survived three years in a North Korean prison camp and was awarded the Victoria Cross; his citation described his leadership as having sustained the battalion's resistance beyond any reasonable expectation. The American Presidential Unit Citation given to the Gloucestershire Regiment noted that their stand had prevented the Chinese breakthrough from reaching Seoul. Whether three days on Hill 235 changed the outcome of the Korean War is the kind of question historians resist — but the 29th Brigade's losses over those three days, 1,091 killed, wounded, or missing, were the heaviest of any Commonwealth brigade in the entire conflict.

onThisDay.headline: German Army Group C Surrenders in Italy
onThisDay.summary: On May 2, 1945, German Army Group C under General Heinrich von Vietinghoff surrendered unconditionally to Allied forces in Italy, ending the Italian campaign of the Second World War. More than one million German and Italian fascist troops laid down arms — the largest single Axis capitulation of the war. The formal surrender had been signed at Caserta on April 29, the culmination of secret negotiations between SS General Karl Wolff and OSS representative Allen Dulles conducted in Switzerland since February.
